```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(stringr)
library(plotly)
library(WDI)
library(here)

options(scipen = 999)
dir.create(here("blog", "posts", "post7", "data"), showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
```

# The question

When prices take off, a central bank has one basic lever: raise its policy
interest rate faster than inflation, so that holding money actually costs
something. When the rate stays *below* inflation, the "real" (inflation-adjusted)
rate is negative — money is effectively free, and the bank is, in the market's
phrase, **behind the curve**.

The 2021–2023 inflation surge was the first worldwide test of that reflex in
forty years. This post asks a simple, concrete question: **as inflation climbed,
which central banks kept their policy rate ahead of it, and which fell behind — and
how fast did they catch up?** One interactive chart answers it, because the answer
is really about *movement* over time, which a single still image can't show.

# The data

Two series, both pulled straight from source in code:

- **Policy rates** come from the Bank for International Settlements (BIS), which
  collects the headline policy rate of about 38 central banks. I download the full
  dataset as a single file and take each country's rate at year-end.
- **Inflation** is annual consumer-price inflation from the World Bank (WDI
  indicator `FP.CPI.TOTL.ZG`), read through the `WDI` package.

The one transformation that matters is the **real policy rate = policy rate −
inflation**. A country sits *above* the 45-degree line when its rate beats
inflation (real rate positive); *below* it when inflation is winning (real rate
negative).

```{r}
#| label: load-data

refresh <- FALSE

# --- Policy rates: BIS bulk file (download once, then cache) ----------------
zip_path <- here("blog", "posts", "post7", "data", "cbpol.zip")
bis_csv  <- here("blog", "posts", "post7", "data", "bis_cbpol.csv")

if (!refresh && file.exists(bis_csv)) {
  bis_raw <- read_csv(bis_csv, show_col_types = FALSE)
} else {
  download.file("https://data.bis.org/static/bulk/WS_CBPOL_csv_flat.zip",
                zip_path, mode = "wb")
  inner <- unzip(zip_path, list = TRUE)$Name[1]
  unzip(zip_path, exdir = here("blog", "posts", "post7", "data"))
  bis_raw <- read_csv(here("blog", "posts", "post7", "data", inner),
                      show_col_types = FALSE)
  write_csv(bis_raw, bis_csv)
}

# BIS columns carry colons/spaces, e.g. `REF_AREA:Reference area` = "US: United States".
policy <- bis_raw |>
  transmute(
    freq    = `FREQ:Frequency`,
    iso2c   = str_extract(`REF_AREA:Reference area`, "^[^:]+"),
    period  = `TIME_PERIOD:Time period or range`,
    rate    = as.numeric(`OBS_VALUE:Observation Value`)
  ) |>
  filter(str_detect(freq, "^M"), str_detect(period, "^[0-9]{4}-[0-9]{2}$")) |>
  mutate(year = as.integer(str_sub(period, 1, 4)),
         month = as.integer(str_sub(period, 6, 7))) |>
  filter(!is.na(rate)) |>
  group_by(iso2c, year) |>
  slice_max(month, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>   # year-end policy rate
  ungroup() |>
  select(iso2c, year, policy_rate = rate)

# --- Inflation: World Bank via WDI (cache the same way) ---------------------
wdi_csv <- here("blog", "posts", "post7", "data", "wdi_inflation.csv")
if (!refresh && file.exists(wdi_csv)) {
  infl <- read_csv(wdi_csv, show_col_types = FALSE)
} else {
  infl <- WDI(indicator = "FP.CPI.TOTL.ZG", start = 2010, end = 2025)
  write_csv(infl, wdi_csv)
}
infl <- infl |>
  transmute(iso2c, country, year = as.integer(year),
            inflation = FP.CPI.TOTL.ZG)

# --- Join, classify, and keep a readable window ----------------------------
advanced <- c("US","JP","GB","CH","SE","NO","DK","CA","AU","NZ","KR","IL")

panel <- policy |>
  inner_join(infl, by = c("iso2c", "year")) |>
  filter(!is.na(inflation), year >= 2015, year <= 2024) |>
  filter(inflation <= 20, policy_rate <= 20) |>   # drop hyperinflation off-scale
  mutate(
    real_rate = policy_rate - inflation,
    group = if_else(iso2c %in% advanced, "Advanced economy", "Emerging economy"),
    hover = paste0("<b>", country, "</b>",
                   "<br>Policy rate: ", sprintf("%.2f", policy_rate), "%",
                   "<br>Inflation: ",   sprintf("%.2f", inflation), "%",
                   "<br>Real rate: ",   sprintf("%+.2f", real_rate), "%")
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: prose-stats
#| include: false

n_banks   <- panel |> filter(year == 2024) |> distinct(iso2c) |> nrow()
yrs       <- sort(unique(panel$year))

behind <- panel |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(n = n(), behind = sum(real_rate < 0), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(share = behind / n)

b2021 <- behind |> filter(year == 2021)
b2022 <- behind |> filter(year == 2022)
b2024 <- behind |> filter(year == 2024)

share_pct <- function(x) paste0(round(100 * x), "%")
```

# The answer, in one moving chart

Each dot is a central bank; drag the slider or press play to move through the
years. The dashed line is where the policy rate exactly equals inflation. **Below
the line, the real rate is negative — the bank is behind the curve.** Hover any dot
to read the country and its exact numbers; click a legend entry to isolate advanced
or emerging economies.

```{r}
#| label: fig-animated
#| column: page

ax <- list(range = c(-1, 20), zeroline = FALSE, ticksuffix = "%")
diag <- data.frame(x = c(-1, 20), y = c(-1, 20))

plot_ly() |>
  add_lines(data = diag, x = ~x, y = ~y,
            line = list(dash = "dash", color = "grey"),
            hoverinfo = "skip", showlegend = FALSE) |>
  add_markers(data = panel, x = ~inflation, y = ~policy_rate,
              frame = ~year, color = ~group,
              colors = c("Advanced economy" = "#2c7fb8",
                         "Emerging economy" = "#c0392b"),
              text = ~hover, hoverinfo = "text",
              marker = list(size = 11, opacity = 0.8,
                            line = list(width = 0.5, color = "white"))) |>
  layout(
    title = list(text = "Policy rate vs. inflation — below the line is behind the curve"),
    xaxis = c(ax, list(title = "Inflation (%)")),
    yaxis = c(ax, list(title = "Policy rate (%)")),
    legend = list(orientation = "h", x = 0, y = 1.05)
  ) |>
  animation_opts(frame = 900, transition = 400, redraw = FALSE) |>
  animation_slider(currentvalue = list(prefix = "Year: "))
```

The animation makes the common story visible as motion. Through 2015–2020 most
dots sit near or above the line — quiet inflation, modestly positive real rates.
Then in **2021** the whole cloud slides *down and to the right*: inflation jumped
but policy rates hadn't moved, so **`r b2021$behind` of `r b2021$n`** central banks
(`r share_pct(b2021$share)`) were below the line, real rates negative. By **2022**
that was **`r b2022$behind` of `r b2022$n`** (`r share_pct(b2022$share)`) — nearly
everyone behind the curve at once. The catch-up is just as clear: by **2024** the
cloud has climbed back above the line, with only **`r b2024$behind` of `r b2024$n`**
(`r share_pct(b2024$share)`) still negative.

One group moved first. If you isolate the emerging economies in the legend, several
Latin American banks (hover to find Brazil and Mexico) were already lifting rates
in 2021, ahead of the Fed and the ECB. That ordering is the kind of detail a static
snapshot hides and the slider surfaces.

# Who caught up, and who sat still

The second chart zooms in on the *real* policy rate — the vertical distance from
that line — for five central banks over time. Hover to read values; click names in
the legend to compare any subset.

```{r}
#| label: fig-realrate

focus <- panel |>
  filter(iso2c %in% c("US","GB","JP","BR","MX")) |>
  mutate(country = recode(country, "United States" = "US",
                          "United Kingdom" = "UK"))

plot_ly(focus, x = ~year, y = ~real_rate, color = ~country,
        type = "scatter", mode = "lines+markers",
        hovertemplate = "%{fullData.name}<br>%{x}: %{y:+.2f}%<extra></extra>") |>
  layout(
    title = list(text = "Real policy rate (policy rate minus inflation)"),
    xaxis = list(title = NULL, dtick = 1),
    yaxis = list(title = "Real policy rate (%)", ticksuffix = "%", zeroline = TRUE),
    shapes = list(list(type = "line", x0 = min(focus$year), x1 = max(focus$year),
                       y0 = 0, y1 = 0, line = list(color = "grey", dash = "dot"))),
    legend = list(orientation = "h", x = 0, y = 1.05)
  )
```

Isolating Brazil shows the sharpest version of the pattern: a deeply negative real
rate in 2021 followed by aggressive hikes that pushed it well above zero by 2023 —
the textbook "get ahead of it" response. The US and UK lines stay below zero a year
longer before climbing back. Japan barely moves: its inflation never rose far, so
its real rate drifted without the dramatic dive-and-recover the others show.

# Takeaway

Across these central banks, 2021–2022 was a near-synchronized slip below the line —
most of the world ran negative real policy rates at the same time — followed by a
two-year climb back above it. The interactive view earns its keep here: the single
number that matters, the gap between a policy rate and inflation, is one most
readers can't picture from a table, but can read instantly as a dot's distance from
a diagonal, and can watch move year by year.

Two honest limits. Year-end annual figures smooth over the exact month each bank
moved, so the chart shows the direction of the catch-up, not its precise timing.
And a positive real rate is not automatically "enough" — how high rates must go
depends on each economy, which this simple comparison doesn't judge.

---

*Data sources: central bank policy rates from the Bank for International
Settlements (`WS_CBPOL`, bulk CSV, read programmatically and cached in `data/`);
consumer-price inflation from the World Bank via the `WDI` package
(`FP.CPI.TOTL.ZG`). A few hyperinflation cases are kept off the 0–20% scale for
readability. Code to reproduce is in the linked GitHub repository.*
